summary: This document defines UTF-8 text representations for IPFIX abstract data types. This supports interoperable use of IPFIX Information Elements in protocols that use textual encodings.

eli5.summary: IPFIX reports network traffic in compact computer code. This RFC explains how to write the same facts as plain readable text, so other tools can understand them.

questions: how to write ipfix data types as text
subtitle: How to write IPFIX flow data types as plain, human-readable text for JSON, XML and similar formats.

tldr.problem: IPFIX defines a compact binary encoding for its data types, but newer management protocols and applications often use text formats such as JSON or XML and still want to use the same Information Elements.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a textual form, written in ABNF, for each IPFIX abstract data type, and tells implementations to defer to the enclosing format's own representation when it has one.
tldr.outcome: Text-based applications can describe flow data using the IPFIX Information Element names and interoperate with IPFIX at the definition level. The encodings favour readability over compactness and are not meant for data storage.

today: RFC 7373 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it says that future abstract data types added to the IPFIX Information Model would require this document to be updated.

sections.title: Why a Text Form Is Needed
sections.content:
The IPFIX Information Model (RFC 7012) gives a set of abstract data types (ADTs) for the IANA "IPFIX Information Elements" registry. The IPFIX protocol (RFC 7011) defines a big-endian binary encoding for them.

Other operations and management protocols may use textual encodings with generic framing and structure, such as JSON (RFC 7159) or XML. A canonical text form for the ADTs lets those applications use the IPFIX Information Elements and interoperate with IPFIX applications at the Information Element definition level.

Templating and other ways of describing data are application specific and out of scope: only Information Element identification and value representation are defined. The RFC makes an explicit trade-off for human readability and manipulability over compactness.
sections.eli5: Computers that talk in compact byte-code and computers that talk in readable text need a shared dictionary. This RFC is the dictionary for writing IPFIX facts in readable text.

sections.title: Identifying Elements by Name
sections.content:
The registry numbers each Information Element with an identifier and also gives it a human-readable name. The numbers are meant for the IPFIX protocol and "have little meaning" in a textual representation.

Text-based applications therefore identify an Information Element by its name, such as octetDeltaCount, not its number.

The RFC also defines the term Enclosing Context: the outer textual format (for example XML or JSON) that carries the values. The Enclosing Context sets the escaping and quoting rules for represented values.
sections.eli5: On a class list you call a kid by name, not by a locker number. In text form, each kind of measurement is called by its name.

sections.title: Binary Data and Numbers
sections.content:
The pattern across the whole RFC is the same: if the Enclosing Context already has a representation for a kind of value (binary objects, unsigned integers, signed integers, floating-point numbers, booleans), that representation SHOULD be used. The RFC's own rules apply otherwise.

octetArray values are strings of hexadecimal digit pairs, one pair per byte, in the order the bytes would appear on the wire. Whitespace between pairs is allowed.

Unsigned integers (unsigned8 to unsigned64) are unprefixed decimal, 0x-prefixed hexadecimal, or 0b-prefixed binary. Leading zeroes never mean octal, and binary is intended for flag-like elements. When an unsigned element identifies a set of codepoints, the codepoint's name or short description MAY be used instead. Signed integers are decimal with an optional plus or minus sign, and the form -0 is explicitly allowed and equals zero.

Out-of-range integers are interpreted as clipped to the range of the type or Information Element.

float32 and float64 use decimal numbers with an optional sign and optional exponent (at most three digits), plus the special strings NaN, +inf and -inf. Writers MAY sacrifice precision for readability, so decoders MUST NOT assume values compare exactly equal.
sections.eli5: Whole numbers can be written the normal way, or in base 16 or base 2 if you want. Very long raw data is written two hex digits at a time. Decimal numbers can lose a tiny bit of exactness, so do not expect them to match perfectly.

sections.title: Text, Time and Address Types
sections.content:
boolean is the literal true or false. A macAddress is six hexadecimal bytes separated by colons, most significant byte first.

string values are Unicode text written directly, using the Enclosing Context's own Unicode, quoting and escaping rules. Characters the context cannot represent, or that are reserved in it, MUST be escaped or quoted. The RFC warns that mixed-direction strings should be avoided and that byte-by-byte comparison does not prove two Unicode strings are equivalent.

The four dateTime types follow RFC 3339 with two differences: all times are UTC, so no zone offset is used, and the type decides the precision. dateTimeSeconds has no fraction, while dateTimeMilliseconds, dateTimeMicroseconds and dateTimeNanoseconds add 3, 6 or 9 fractional digits.

ipv4Address is dotted-quad as in RFC 3986. ipv6Address follows Section 2.2 of RFC 4291 as updated by RFC 5952.

The list types basicList, subTemplateList and subTemplateMultiList MUST NOT be used in textual representations, because the enclosing protocol is assumed to provide its own structure.
sections.eli5: True and false are written as the words true and false. Times are written like a calendar date and clock time in one standard time zone. Addresses look the way you already see them, like four numbers separated by dots.

sections.title: A Worked JSON Example
sections.content:
Appendix A shows a flow template in Information Element Specifier (IESpec) format and one data record described by it, written as a JSON object. Each key is an Information Element name, so the record uses flowStartMilliseconds, octetDeltaCount, sourceIPv6Address and so on.

The RFC stresses that this is "specifically NOT a recommendation for a particular representation" and only illustrates the encodings; the quoting and formatting are JSON specific. Note that protocolIdentifier is written as the string tcp, an example of using a codepoint name for an unsigned element.
sections.eli5: The example is a sample report card for one network conversation, written with labels and values so a person can read each line.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Notes
sections.content:
The security considerations of the IPFIX protocol (RFC 7011) apply. Decoders must handle invalid input correctly, though these encodings are not special in that respect.

The encoding is specifically not intended for storage of data. Because text is easy to index and search, privacy-sensitive traffic data could be indexed or searched by accident, so the privacy considerations of RFC 7011 are especially important when storing such data. The RFC suggests omitting sensitive values entirely, as in black-marker anonymization from RFC 6235.

All types except string can be written in US-ASCII. The string type can be vulnerable to ill-formed UTF-8 problems.
sections.eli5: Text is easy to search, so private details could be found by mistake. The advice is to leave private parts out when you write the report.
